title: The Elegant Flirt 8
content:
Wei Wuxian returned to the Cloud Recesses loaded down with an assortment of junk he’d picked up in Caiyi Town, which the other disciples promptly stripped clean. With Lan Qiren away in Qinghe, classes were on hold for a few days, and the boys took full advantage—partying like there was no tomorrow. They crammed into Wei Wuxian and Jiang Cheng’s room to crash on the floor, spending the nights drinking, arm-wrestling, rolling dice, and flipping through illustrated booklets. One evening, Wei Wuxian lost a bet on the dice and was dispatched over the wall to smuggle back some Emperor’s Smile, finally treating everyone to a proper drink. Come morning, long before dawn, the room was still littered with teenagers splayed out like corpses when someone suddenly slid the door open.

The click of the latch startled a few awake. Bleary-eyed, they caught sight of Lan Wangji standing in the doorway, face colder than winter frost, and jolted sober in an instant. Nie Huaisang scrambled over, frantically shaking Wei Wuxian, who was snoring upside down with his head where his feet should be: “Wei-xiong! Wei-xiong!”

Jostled awake, Wei Wuxian mumbled half-asleep, “Who is it? Who else wants a go?! Jiang Cheng? Bring it on, you think I’m scared of you?!”

Nursing a vicious hangover, Jiang Cheng kept his eyes squeezed shut, reached for the first object within arm's reach, and hurled it toward the noise. “Shut up!”

The missile struck Wei Wuxian dead in the chest, pages fluttering wildly. Nie Huaisang looked closer—it was one of his prized, out-of-print erotic art folios. Looking back up at Lan Wangji’s razor-sharp glare, Nie Huaisang felt his soul almost leave his body. Wei Wuxian simply hugged the book, mumbled something under his breath, and drifted back to sleep. Lan Wangji stepped into the room, caught him by the back of his collar, hoisted him up, and began dragging him out the door.

Dangled like a scruffed cat, Wei Wuxian finally came to his senses. He twisted around, squinting. “Lan Zhan, what are you doing?”

Lan Wangji didn't say a word, marching forward with his captive in tow. Wei Wuxian sobered up a little more, while the rest of the boys on the floor began stumbling awake one by one. Seeing Wei Wuxian being hauled away by the scruff again, Jiang Cheng charged out of the room. “What’s going on? What are you doing with him?”

Lan Wangji glanced back, clipping each syllable: “Receiving punishment.”

Jiang Cheng’s booze-addled brain finally caught up. Remembering the wreckage strewn across their floor, and the sheer volume of Lan clan rules they had shredded the night before, his face went completely rigid.

Lan Wangji dragged Wei Wuxian to the courtyard fronting the Gusu Lan ancestral hall. Eight senior disciples stood waiting in silence. Four of them held extraordinarily long sandalwood disciplinary rulers carved with dense, tiny script, their faces severe and unyielding. The moment Lan Wangji arrived with his quarry, two disciples stepped forward and pinned Wei Wuxian firmly down. Forced onto his knees, Wei Wuxian struggled against their grip. “Lan Zhan, you’re really punishing me?”

Lan Wangji met his eyes with a chill, saying nothing.

Wei Wuxian dug in his heels. “I don't accept this.”

By now, the rest of the boys had scrambled over, half-awake and hovering anxiously outside the courtyard. Barred from entering, they wrung their hands and winced at the sight of the heavy rulers. Then, to everyone’s shock, Lan Wangji gathered the hem of his white robes and dropped to his knees right beside Wei Wuxian.

Wei Wuxian’s eyes went wide. He scrambled to get up, but Lan Wangji barked the order: “Strike!”

Stunned, Wei Wuxian panicked. “Wait, wait, wait! I accept! I accept, Lan Zhan, I was wro—gah!”

Both took over a hundred strikes across the palms and calves. Lan Wangji needed no one to hold him down; his spine remained rod-straight, his posture immaculate throughout. Wei Wuxian, by contrast, wailed like a slaughtered pig without an ounce of shame, making the watching disciples wince and cringe with every crack of wood on flesh. When the flogging finished, Lan Wangji rose quietly, bowed to the attending disciples, and walked away without showing a trace of pain. Wei Wuxian was the exact opposite. Slumped over Jiang Cheng’s back as he was carried out, he moaned the entire way. The other boys crowded around in a flurry of whispers: “Wei-xiong, what happened?”

“Lan Zhan punishing you is one thing, but why did he get beaten too?”

Wei Wuxian buried his face in Jiang Cheng’s shoulder, sighing dramatically. “Ah! A total miscalculation! It’s a long story!”

Jiang Cheng snapped, “Cut the crap! What did you actually do?!”

Wei Wuxian protested, “Nothing! You know I lost the bet last night and went down the mountain for Emperor’s Smile, right?”

Jiang Cheng pinched the bridge of his nose. “...Don't tell me you ran into him again.”

“Spot on,” Wei Wuxian said. “Talk about rotten luck. I was vaulting the wall with the jars on my shoulder and ran smack into him. I’m convinced the guy spends his entire day staking me out.”

Jiang Cheng scoffed. “You think everyone’s as idle as you are? Then what?”

Wei Wuxian went on, “So I greeted him like usual: ‘Lan Zhan! What a coincidence, you again!’ Naturally, he ignored me completely and threw a palm strike right at my chest. I said, ‘Hey, what’s the rush?’ He told me that repeated curfew violations meant going to the ancestral hall for punishment. So I told him, ‘Look, it’s just the two of us here. If you don’t tell and I don’t tell, nobody knows I broke curfew, right? I swear this is the last time. We’re practically best friends by now—can’t you cut me some slack?’”

The surrounding boys wore matching looks of pure secondhand embarrassment.

Wei Wuxian continued, “Then he pulled that stiff face, insisted we weren't friends, and drew his sword. Completely heartless! So I had to set the jars aside and trade blows with him. He was relentlessly aggressive, throwing punches and palms—I couldn't shake him off! Finally, I lost my patience. I said, ‘Are you really not letting this go? Truly not letting go?!’

“And he still just said: ‘Receive punishment!’”

The disciples hung on every word, their breath catching. Wei Wuxian’s eyes lit up as he told the tale, entirely forgetting he was clinging to Jiang Cheng’s back. He brought an open palm down hard on Jiang Cheng’s shoulder. “So I said, ‘Fine!’ I stopped dodging, lunged forward, grabbed him in a bear hug, and tackled us both right over the perimeter wall!”

The clearing fell dead silent.

Wei Wuxian grinned. “And just like that, we tumbled outside the Cloud Recesses together! Saw stars when we hit the dirt, I swear.”

Nie Huaisang stared blankly. “...He didn't shake you off?”

“Oh, he tried,” Wei Wuxian said. “Wrapped my arms and legs around him in a vice grip, though. He was stiff as a board, couldn't push off me at all. So I told him: ‘How about that, Lan Zhan? Now you’re outside the boundary too! We’re both breaking curfew. You can’t be strict with others and lenient with yourself—if you punish me, you have to take the hits too. Equal treatment, fair?’

“His face was pitch-black when he got up. I sat in the grass and told him, ‘Don’t worry, I won’t rat you out. What happens between us stays between us.’ He didn’t say a word and just walked off. Who knew he’d pull this stunt at dawn... Hey, Jiang Cheng, slow down, you’re about to shake me off!”

Forget shaking him off—Jiang Cheng looked ready to spike him headfirst into the pavers. “I carry you and you complain?!”

Wei Wuxian retorted, “I didn’t ask you to carry me in the first place.”

Jiang Cheng flared up. “If I didn't carry you, you’d still be rolling on their ancestral hall floor pretending to be crippled, throwing our face away! Lan Wangji took fifty more strikes than you did and walked off under his own power. Have some shame! I’m done carrying you—get off!”

Wei Wuxian clung tighter. “Not getting down. I’m an invalid.”

The group bickered and jostled their way down the white gravel path until a figure in pristine white robes, carrying a scroll under his arm, stepped around the bend and paused in surprise. Lan Xichen offered a warm smile. “What is the matter here?”

Jiang Cheng froze, mortified, scrambling for an excuse. But Nie Huaisang blurted out first, “Xichen-ge, Wei-xiong just took over a hundred strikes from the disciplinary ruler! Do you have any medicine?”

Discipline in the Cloud Recesses fell squarely under Lan Wangji’s purview. Hearing that and seeing Wei Wuxian groaning in the center of the crowd like a dying man, Lan Xichen stepped forward immediately, his tone laced with concern. “Wangji disciplined him? Young Master Wei cannot walk? What happened?”

Jiang Cheng couldn't very well admit the truth—it was their whole crew that had bribed Wei Wuxian to smuggle liquor, and admitting it meant dragging everyone down with him. He mumbled defensively, “It's nothing, really! Not that dramatic! He can walk fine. Wei Wuxian, get down already!”

“I can't walk,” Wei Wuxian whined. He held up a hand swollen bright red like a steamed bun, lodging his complaint to Lan Xichen: “Ze-wu-jun, your brother is far too ruthless.”

Lan Xichen inspected the palm. “Ah... that truly is quite severe. I fear the swelling will not subside for three or four days.”

Jiang Cheng hadn't realized the beating was that bad. “What? Three or four days? He took hits to his back and calves too! How could Lan Wangji be this heavy-handed?!”

The complaint slipped out before he could filter it. Wei Wuxian gave him a sharp jab in the ribs, jolting him back to his senses. Lan Xichen took no offense, smiling gently. “No matter. Ointments won't be necessary; I know a remedy that will heal it in just a few hours.”

That evening, the Cold Spring of the Cloud Recesses lay shrouded in mist.

Lan Wangji sat submerged in the icy water, eyes closed in meditation, when a voice piped up right beside his ear: “Lan Zhan.”

Lan Wangji’s eyes snapped open.

Sure enough, Wei Wuxian was sprawled across the flat blue stone at the water's edge, resting his chin in his hand, grinning down at him.

Lan Wangji couldn't hold back the question: “How did you get in here?!”

Wei Wuxian picked himself up languidly, undoing his sash. “Ze-wu-jun told me to come.”

Lan Wangji frowned. “What are you doing?”

Wei Wuxian kicked off his boots, letting his robes tumble onto the grass in a careless pile. “I’m taking off my clothes—what do you think I’m doing? Word is your cold spring soothes the mind for cultivation and heals bruises on the side, so your brother told me to hop in with you. Honestly, sneaking off to treat your wounds alone is a bit stingy, don't you think? Whoa, that is freezing! Hiss—”

The second he hit the water, the bone-chilling cold sent him thrashing and paddling around the pool. Lan Wangji put three paces between them instantly. “I came here to meditate, not to treat wounds—stop splashing!”

Wei Wuxian shivered. “B-but it’s freezing! It’s ridiculously cold!”

He wasn't hamming it up this time. To an outsider, the Lan clan’s Cold Spring was brutal, feeling as though lingering still for more than a second would turn your blood to slush. He flailed around frantically, desperate to kickstart his circulation. Lan Wangji, who had been completely at peace moments ago, was now catching cold droplets across his face, water trickling down his wet lashes and dark hair. Reaching his limit, he barked, “Stop moving!”

He reached out and planted a firm palm against Wei Wuxian’s shoulder.

A rush of warm spiritual energy surged through the point of contact, instantly taking the edge off the bitter chill. Relieved, Wei Wuxian instinctively leaned closer.

Lan Wangji tensed. “What are you doing?”

Wei Wuxian blinked with wide-eyed innocence. “Nothing! Just seems warmer over by you.”

Lan Wangji kept his arm locked between them like a barricade. “It is not.”

Wei Wuxian had only wanted to close the distance and butter him up; finding himself stonewalled, he took the rejection in stride. His eyes wandered to Lan Wangji’s hands and bare shoulders. The red welts were still clearly visible. He really hadn't come here for the healing properties.

Wei Wuxian sighed with genuine awe. “Lan Zhan, I really do hand it to you. When you say punishment, you really take the cane right alongside the culprit—not a drop of favoritism. I’m speechless.”

Lan Wangji closed his eyes again, returning to stone-faced silence.

Wei Wuxian pressed on. “Seriously, I’ve never met someone as stubbornly upright as you. A man of your word down to the bone. I could never pull that off. You’re incredible.”

Lan Wangji gave no reply.

Once his body adjusted to the chill, Wei Wuxian began paddling lazy laps around the pool. After a minute, he circled back, leaning in close. “Lan Zhan, did you seriously miss what I was doing just now?”

“I have no idea,” Lan Wangji said flatly.

Wei Wuxian threw his hands up. “How could you miss it? I was praising you! Flattering you! Trying to get on your good side!”

Lan Wangji glanced at him. “What is your angle?”

“Lan Zhan, let’s be friends,” Wei Wuxian coaxed. “We know each other so well by now.”

“We do not.”

Wei Wuxian slapped the surface, sending ripples across the pool. “You’re no fun at all. Truly. Being friends with me has a ton of perks!”

Lan Wangji leveled a flat stare. “Such as?”

Wei Wuxian drifted to the edge, resting his elbows on the stone ledge. “I treat my friends right. For starters, whenever I get my hands on fresh erotic prints, you get first pick... Hey, hey! Don’t swim away! Fine, forget the art! Have you ever been to Yunmeng? Yunmeng is a blast! And the food is incredible. I don't know if it’s a Gusu thing or just a Cloud Recesses problem, but your food is borderline inedible. If you come visit Lotus Pier, you can eat like a king. I’ll take you out to pick lotus pods and water caltrops! Lan Zhan, what do you say?”

“I will not go,” Lan Wangji stated.

Wei Wuxian chided, “Don’t always lead with ‘no’! You sound so cold. Girls won’t like that. The maidens in Yunmeng are gorgeous too, totally different from the gentle beauties down here in Gusu.” He flashed a playful wink. “Sure you don't want to come?”

Lan Wangji hesitated for a fraction of a second, then doubled down: “No—”

Wei Wuxian cut in, “Keep brushing me off like this and I might just take your clothes when I leave.”

Lan Wangji snapped: “Get out!”

When Lan Qiren returned from Qinghe, he didn’t bother banishing Wei Wuxian back to the Library Pavilion to copy rules. Instead, he subjected him to a blistering tirade in front of the entire assembly. Stripping away the endless classical quotations and moral treatises, the lecture boiled down to one simple sentiment: I have never in my life witnessed a student so rotten, incorrigible, and shameless. Get out, pack your bags, and get as far away from my sight as possible. Stay away from the other disciples, and above all, stop polluting my star pupil, Lan Wangji.

Wei Wuxian had listened to the entire scolding with a broad, beaming grin, showing neither shame nor remorse. The moment Lan Qiren marched out, Wei Wuxian dropped into his seat, leaning toward Jiang Cheng. “Telling me to keep my distance now? A bit late for that! The boy’s already thoroughly corrupted—too late to save him!”

Down in Caiyi Town, the Waterborne Abyss was causing endless headaches for the Gusu Lan Sect. The anomaly couldn't be permanently eradicated, and unlike the Qishan Wen Clan, the Lan Sect refused to displace the curse into neighboring waters. With the Clan Leader in deep seclusion, dealing with the fallout drained Lan Qiren’s time and energy. His lectures grew progressively shorter, leaving Wei Wuxian with plenty of free time to lead the other boys roaming the mountains.

One afternoon, flanked by a half-dozen disciples on their way out, Wei Wuxian passed beneath the Library Pavilion. Peeking up through the leafy branches of the magnolia tree, he caught sight of Lan Wangji sitting alone by the open window.

Nie Huaisang scratched his chin, bewildered. “Is he looking over here? That's weird—we weren't even being loud. What’s with that glare?”

Wei Wuxian chuckled. “Probably racking his brain trying to figure out how to catch us slipping.”

Jiang Cheng scoffed. “Wrong. Not 'us'—you. He’s staring straight at you.”

Wei Wuxian grinned. “Heh. Just wait. Watch how I handle him when we get back.”

Jiang Cheng warned, “Didn't you complain he was boring and stiff? Leave him alone. You’re pulling whiskers from a tiger’s mouth, dancing on a landmine. You court death every waking hour.”

Wei Wuxian shook his finger. “Wrong again! The fact that a living, breathing human being can actually be thatboring—that’s what makes him endlessly fascinating!”

They didn't wander back to the Cloud Recesses until near noon. Lan Wangji was sitting upright at his low desk, smoothing out a fresh stack of completed calligraphy, when a faint tapping rattled the lattice. He looked up just as a figure hoisted himself over the sill.

Wei Wuxian hopped down from the magnolia branches outside, beaming ear-to-ear. “Lan Zhan, I’m back! Well? A few days without me copying texts—did you miss me?”

Lan Wangji sat like a meditating monk, staring straight through him, then went back to squaring his neat towers of scrolls with numb resignation. Wei Wuxian gleefully twisted the silence: “You don’t have to say it out loud, I already know. You totally missed me! Why else would you be staring out the window watching me earlier?”

Lan Wangji’s eyes snapped to his, burning with silent condemnation.

Wei Wuxian hopped up to perch casually on the windowsill. “Look at you, taking the bait after two sentences. So easy to rattle. Zero patience.”

“Leave,” Lan Wangji clipped.

Wei Wuxian countered, “And if I don’t? Going to shove me out?”

Taking in the cold fire in Lan Wangji’s eyes, Wei Wuxian figured one more word really would snap the boy's legendary restraint and get himself spiked to the sill. He held up his hands in mock surrender. “All right, don't look at me like that! I came bearing gifts to make amends.”

Lan Wangji didn't hesitate. “I do not want it.”

Wei Wuxian coaxed, “Really? Sure you don't?” Seeing the flicker of suspicion in Lan Wangji’s gaze, he reached into his robes like a street magician and pulled out two rabbits by their scruffs. They looked like a pair of plump, snow-white pom-poms, their back paws kicking randomly in midair. He dangled them right under Lan Wangji’s nose. “Your mountain is weird—not a pheasant in sight, but it’s crawling with wild rabbits that aren't even afraid of people. Look at them, nice and fat! Want one?”

Lan Wangji stared at him with total indifference.

Wei Wuxian shrugged. “Fine then. If you don't want them, I’ll give them to someone else. I’ve been craving meat lately anyway.”

Hearing that, Lan Wangji’s voice sharpened: “Halt.”

Wei Wuxian spread his hands. “I haven't moved an inch.”

Lan Wangji demanded, “Who do you intend to give them to?”

Wei Wuxian replied, “Whoever’s best at roasting rabbit meat.”

Lan Wangji’s voice turned rigid: “Taking of life is forbidden within the Cloud Recesses. It is the third rule on the Wall of Discipline.”

Wei Wuxian waved it off. “Easy fix. I’ll take them down the mountain, slaughter them outside the boundary, and haul them back up to grill. You didn't want them anyway, so why do you care?”

Lan Wangji’s jaw set. Every word was forced through his teeth: “...Give them to me.”

Perched on the sill, Wei Wuxian burst out laughing. “Backpedaling already? Look at you, always like this.”

Both rabbits were round and fluffy, like two balls of fresh snow. One had sleepy, dead-fish eyes, sprawling lazily on the floorboards without twitching for minutes at a time, chewing its leafy greens with slow, delicate twitches of its pink nose. The other was an absolute live wire, bouncing off the walls, scrambling over its companion, twisting and kicking in a ceaseless flurry of energy. Wei Wuxian tossed down a few vegetable scraps he’d scavenged from somewhere, then suddenly blurted out: “Lan Zhan! Lan Zhan, look!”

The hyperactive rabbit had just stepped directly into Lan Wangji’s inkstone, leaving a trail of wet black paw prints across the pristine wooden desk. Lan Wangji, paralyzed with dismay, was holding a scrap of paper trying to figure out how to clean it without making a mess. He hadn't planned on taking the bait, but the sheer gravity in Wei Wuxian’s voice made him think something was actually wrong. “What is it?”

Wei Wuxian pointed. “Look at how they’re stacked up! Are they...?”

Lan Wangji’s voice cracked with icy finality: “They are both male!”

Wei Wuxian blinked in exaggerated shock. “Both bucks? Well, that’s bizarre!” He scooped them up by the ears to check, confirming the fact. “Huh, they really are bucks. Male or not, I hadn't even finished my sentence—why are you snapping at me? What were you picturing? Come to think of it, I’m the one who caught them and I didn't even check their sex. How did you know their—”

Lan Wangji finally lost it and shoved him straight out the window.

Mid-fall, Wei Wuxian’s obnoxious laughter echoed across the courtyard: “Hahahahahahahahahahahahaha!”

Slam!

Lan Wangji wrenched the window shut, sinking back onto his floor mat by the desk.

He surveyed the scene: crumpled paper everywhere, black ink tracks across the grain, and two white bunnies rolling across the floor chasing wilted cabbage leaves. He closed his eyes and clamped his hands tightly over his ears.

The trembling magnolia branches were locked outside the pane. But no matter how hard he tried to shut it out, Wei Wuxian’s wild, bright laughter slipped through the cracks all the same.

The next day, Lan Wangji stopped attending lectures altogether.

Wei Wuxian’s seat had already migrated three times. He had originally shared a low desk with Jiang Cheng, but Jiang Cheng took his studies seriously; determined to perform well and bring honor to the Yunmeng Jiang Clan, Jiang Cheng sat in the front row. The spot was far too exposed for any slacking, so Wei Wuxian had abandoned him to camp out directly behind Lan Wangji. Sitting behind Lan Wangji was prime real estate: the boy sat upright like a solid iron fortress, leaving Wei Wuxian free to snooze or doodle unnoticed, only occasionally interrupted when Lan Wangji’s hand whipped back to intercept a stray paper ball mid-flight. But Lan Qiren had quickly sniffed out the scheme and swapped their seats front-to-back. From that day on, the moment Wei Wuxian slumped even an inch, two piercing, icy daggers would bore into his spine from behind, mirrored by Lan Qiren’s venomous scowls from the podium. Trapped between the old master and the young prodigy, he’d been monitored every second of the day.

Then came the erotic manual incident, followed swiftly by the twin rabbits debacle. Convinced Wei Wuxian was a vat of moral dye that would stain anyone within arm's reach, Lan Qiren rushed to pull his star pupil from the class entirely before he could be corrupted. Wei Wuxian drifted back to his original seat, enjoying half a month of peaceful quiet.

Unfortunately, for someone like Wei Wuxian, peace was always a fleeting illusion.

Running through the grounds of the Cloud Recesses stood an openwork corridor wall, inset with hollow carved lattice screens every seven paces. Each stone relief depicted a different scene: plucking a zither atop a mountain peak, riding a sword through the clouds, or slaying legendary beasts. Lan Qiren explained that every window along the wall recorded a pivotal milestone from the life of a prominent Gusu Lan ancestor. The oldest and most celebrated among them were four panels illustrating the journey of the sect’s founder, Lan An.

Born and raised in a Buddhist temple listening to holy chants, Lan An had been an exceptionally gifted, renowned monk by his youth. Coming of age, he chose the character Lan—from the Buddhist term sangharama—as his family name, renounced his monastic vows, and took up the life of a traveling musician. While seeking the Dao, he arrived in Gusu, where he encountered his fated soulmate. Together, they laid the foundation of the Gusu Lan Clan. Following his cultivation partner's passing, he returned to the monastery to live out his twilight years in quiet contemplation. The four screens were titled The Temple, The Music, The Partner, and The Return.

It was the first genuinely fascinating lecture Lan Qiren had delivered in weeks. Even though the old master had managed to drain all the magic from the tale, reducing it to a dry timeline of dates, Wei Wuxian had actually paid attention.

Stepping out of the pavilion after class, he mused aloud, “To think the Lan Clan’s founder was a monk—makes total sense now. Entering the mortal realm for a single soul, leaving it behind when that soul is gone... not a trace of dust left behind. But how on earth did an ancestor with that much romance end up with descendants this wooden?”

The boys hadn't expected the rigidly disciplined Lan Clan to boast such a colorful pedigree, and chatter erupted instantly. Before long, the conversation drifted toward the topic of cultivation partners, devolving into heated debates about their ideal matches and lively reviews of the various maidens of the great sects.

At one point, someone chimed in, “Zixuan-xiong, which maiden do you think takes the crown?”

Wei Wuxian and Jiang Cheng froze, their heads snapping toward a young master sitting near the front of the pavilion.

The boy carried himself with proud, aristocratic poise, a vermilion cinnabar mark resting squarely between his brows. His collar, sleeves, and sash were exquisitely embroidered with the "Sparks Amidst Snow" white peony of the Lanling Jin Clan—Jin Zixuan, sent to Gusu for his formal schooling.

Another disciple cut in, “Why bother asking Zixuan-xiong? He’s already betrothed! His answer is obviously his future bride.”

Hearing the word betrothed, Jin Zixuan’s lips twitched downward, his expression souring.

The oblivious disciple pressed on cheerfully, “Really? Which clan is she from? She must be exceptionally brilliant!”

Jin Zixuan arched a haughty brow. “Drop it.”

Wei Wuxian’s voice rang out: “What do you mean, ‘drop it’?”

The classroom fell dead silent, heads swiveling in surprise. Wei Wuxian had always been the easygoing clown; even when yelled at or punished, he’d never shown real anger. Yet right now, a sharp, dangerous edge flared behind his eyes. Jiang Cheng hadn't scolded him for stirring up trouble either; he sat beside him, his expression pitch-black.

Jin Zixuan scoffed, “Is the phrase ‘drop it’ that hard to grasp?”

Wei Wuxian smiled coldly. “The words are simple enough. What’s hard to grasp is what grievance you could possibly have against my shijie.”

Whispers rippled through the room as the pieces clicked into place. Those casual questions had kicked a hornets’ nest: Jin Zixuan’s betrothed was none other than Jiang Yanli of the Yunmeng Jiang Clan.

Jiang Yanli was Jiang Fengmian’s eldest daughter and Jiang Cheng’s elder sister. Gentle and unassuming, she lacked dazzling beauty; steady in speech, she possessed little worldly wit. Her looks were merely pleasant, and her cultivation talent was entirely average. Flanked by the vibrant, brilliant maidens of the rival sects, she naturally faded into the background. Her fiancé, by contrast, stood on the opposite end of the spectrum: the only legitimate son of Jin Guangshan, blessed with striking good looks and exceptional talent. By conventional metrics, she simply couldn't hold a candle to him. The only reason the match existed at all was because her mother hailed from the Meishan Yu Clan, whose family had generations of deep ties with Madam Jin’s lineage. The two matriarchs had grown up like sisters and arranged the pact in their youth.

The Jin Clan had always been haughty to a fault, and Jin Zixuan had inherited every ounce of that arrogance. He had despised the arrangement from the start—not just because of the match itself, but because his mother had dictated his future without his consent. Caught in a rebellious streak, today was his breaking point.

Jin Zixuan sneered, “Why don’t you ask what about her could possibly satisfy me?”

Jiang Cheng rose to his feet with a scrape of wood.

Wei Wuxian shoved Jiang Cheng behind him, stepping forward with an icy scoff. “And what makes you think anyone’s satisfied with you? Where do you get the nerve to stand there turning your nose up?!”

Tied down by the unwanted engagement, Jin Zixuan had never held much love for the Yunmeng Jiang Clan, and he’d long loathed Wei Wuxian’s reckless antics. Believing himself superior to his peers, he had never been talked down to like this. The blood rushed to his head, and the venom spilled out: “If she isn't satisfied, tell her to break the betrothal! I have zero interest in your precious shijie anyway! If you want her so badly, go beg her father for her hand yourself! Doesn't he treat you better than his own flesh and blood anyway?!”

At that final sentence, Jiang Cheng’s gaze locked onto the floor.

Wei Wuxian’s vision went red. He lunged across the desks, his fist flying. Jin Zixuan had braced for a scrap, but he hadn't expected the attack to hit with blinding speed before the sentence had even cleared the air. The punch landed flush against his cheek, numbing half his face. Without a word, he swung back.

The brawl blew up into an incident that dragged two great clans into the fray. By nightfall, both Jiang Fengmian and Jin Guangshan had arrived in Gusu from Yunmeng and Lanling respectively.

After checking on the two bruised boys kneeling outside, the clan leaders endured a furious tongue-lashing from Lan Qiren. Wiping the sweat from their brows, they exchanged stiff pleasantries before Jiang Fengmian quietly broached the topic of ending the betrothal.

He looked Jin Guangshan in the eye. “This engagement was pushed through by A-Li’s mother; I never agreed with it from the start. Seeing that neither child is happy with the arrangement, we shouldn't force it.”

Jin Guangshan was taken aback, hesitating. Dissolving a betrothal with another Great Sect was never good for appearances. “Children will be children. Let them bicker, Brother Fengmian—there’s no need for us to take it to heart.”

Jiang Fengmian replied gently, “Brother Jin, we can arrange their betrothals, but we cannot live their lives for them. After all, they are the ones who must share the rest of their days together.”

Jin Guangshan had never cared for the match either. If he wanted to forge political alliances to consolidate power, the Yunmeng Jiang Clan was neither his only option nor his best one; he’d only gone along with it because he never dared cross Madam Jin. Now that the Jiang Clan was offering a way out, the Jin Clan—holding the groom's side—had far less social baggage to worry about. Besides, he knew full well his son couldn't stand Jiang Yanli. Weighing the options, Jin Guangshan swallowed his pride and agreed to dissolve the pact.

Out on the gravel path where Lan Qiren had ordered him to kneel, Wei Wuxian had no idea what his fists had just broken apart.

Jiang Cheng walked up from the distance, his voice dripping with dry sarcasm: “Look at you, kneeling like a good little boy.”

Wei Wuxian grinned through the aches. “You know I’m an old pro at kneeling. But that pampered peacock Jin Zixuan has probably never taken a knee in his life. If he isn't crying for his mommy by sundown, I’ll take his family name.”

Jiang Cheng stared at the stones for a beat, his tone turning quiet. “Father is here.”

Wei Wuxian blinked. “Shijie didn't come, did she?”

Jiang Cheng scoffed. “Why would she? To watch you make a fool of her? If she were here, wouldn't she be sitting right beside you handing out salves?”

Wei Wuxian let out a low sigh. “...It’d be nice if she were here, though. Good thing you didn't throw a punch.”

Jiang Cheng muttered, “I was going to. If you hadn't shoved me out of the way, the other side of his face would be swollen to match.”

“Better this way,” Wei Wuxian laughed. “The lopsided swelling makes him look even uglier. I heard that peacock is obsessed with his own reflection—I wonder what he thinks looking in the mirror right now? Hahaha...” He gave the dirt a hearty smack, then added, “Honestly, I should’ve let you hit him while I just watched. That way Uncle Jiang might not have flown out here. But I couldn't help myself!”

Jiang Cheng let out a soft snort. “Dream on.”

Wei Wuxian had tossed the comment off without thinking, but it left Jiang Cheng’s chest tight with a bitter, tangled knot. Deep down, he knew the truth:

Jiang Fengmian had never dropped everything to fly to another clan for him in a single day. Not for good news, not for bad news; not for triumphs, not for disasters.

Never.

Noticing Jiang Cheng’s darkened mood, Wei Wuxian assumed he was still dwelling on Jin Zixuan’s poisonous words. “Go on, head back. No need to keep me company. If Lan Wangji comes back around, he’ll catch you slacking. Go gawk at that idiot Jin Zixuan kneeling in the gravel instead.”

Jiang Cheng’s eyebrows pulled together. “Lan Wangji? What would he come out here for? He actually dared to show his face to you?”

Wei Wuxian snickered. “Right? I was surprised by his courage too. Probably sent by his uncle to check if I was kneeling straight.”

Jiang Cheng’s gut clenched. “...And were you?”

“I was at first,” Wei Wuxian said, leaning in like a conspirator. “Then once he walked a few paces away, I grabbed a twig and started digging a hole in the dirt right by your boots. There’s an ant nest right there—took me forever to track it down! When he looked back, my shoulders were shaking from digging, so he thought I was sobbing or something and rushed back over to ask what was wrong. Man, you should've seen his face when he looked down and saw the ants.”

Jiang Cheng stared at him with profound exhaustion. “...Pack your bags and get the hell back to Yunmeng. I swear to the gods, that man never wants to lay eyes on you again as long as he lives.”

And so, that very night, Wei Wuxian packed his bags and rolled right back to Yunmeng alongside Jiang Fengmian.
